Chapter 3 72
Summary
In this chapter, you moved from theory to practice and mastered the foundational skills of
version control with Git and GitHub. You learned that Git thinks in snapshots and uses three
trees – the working directory, staging area, and repository – to manage your work. You
practiced the fundamental workflow of git add and git commit, and understood how git
push and git pull are used to synchronize with remote repositories.
We then explored how to manage complexity and enable teamwork using branching,
introducing the structured GitFlow strategy as a powerful model for collaboration. You put it
all together in a hands-on exercise where you created a GitHub repository, cloned it, worked on
a feature branch, and used a pull request to merge your changes, learning about the critical
importance of code reviews in the process. Finally, you faced the inevitable merge conflict and
learned about the step-by-step process to resolve it confidently. These skills are not just about
managing code; they are about enabling the collaborative and automated workflows that are at
the very heart of DevOps.
Professional habits: The Git checklist
Experienced engineers internalize a handful of simple habits that prevent the most
common mistakes. Keep these in mind as you build your daily workflow:
Always run git status before you do anything: It takes two seconds and
tells you exactly where you are, which branch you're on, what's staged, and
what's not. It prevents most "I committed to the wrong branch" incidents.
Write meaningful commit messages: A message such as fix: resolve null
pointer on login page is infinitely more useful than stuff when you're
debugging a production issue at midnight six months from now.
Pull before you push: Always run git pull on your branch before pushing.
This surfaces any conflicts locally where you can resolve them comfortably,
rather than discovering them mid-push.
Never commit directly to main: Always work on a dedicated feature or fix
branch and go through a pull request. This is not just a rule for big teams; it
protects even solo developers by keeping the main branch always in a known-
good state.

Why containers? Understanding the core concept
Before we start typing commands, it's crucial to understand the problem that containers solve.
For decades, a persistent idx_a7d07fc3 and frustrating issue has plagued software development teams: an
application works perfectly on a developer's machine but fails in the testing or production
environment. This leads to friction, delays, and the infamous phrase, " But it works on my
machine! " This section will explore why this problem exists and how containers provide an
elegant and powerful solution.
The challenge of environmental drift
The "it works on my machine" problem is almost always due to subtle differences between
environments. Your laptop is not the same as the company's testing server, which is not the
same as idx_2402d2d8 the production servers running in the cloud. This idx_d4b24d24 difference is known as
environmental drift.
Drift can be caused by many factors. Your laptop might have Python 3.9 installed, while the
production server has Python 3.8. You might have a specific system library installed that the
application depends on, which is missing on the test server. Even minor differences in
operating system patch levels or environment variable configurations can cause an application
to behave unexpectedly or fail entirely. Managing these dependencies and ensuring
consistency across all environments has traditionally been a complex and error-prone manual
process.
To understand how containers address the problem of environmental drift, it helps to first look
at how this challenge was traditionally handled using virtual machines.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 78
chunks.content:
Chapter 4 78
Containers versus virtual machines
For many years, the primary idx_5639337f solution to this problem was the virtual machine (VM). A VM is
an emulation of a complete computer system. A piece of software called a hypervisor runs on idx_d90e3881 a
host machine and allows you to create multiple idx_33750612 guest machines. Each guest VM has its idx_b8595547 own
full copy of an operating system (such as Ubuntu or Windows Server), along with virtualized
hardware. You can then install your application and its dependencies inside this isolated guest
OS. This provides excellent isolation and solves the consistency problem, but it comes at a high
cost.
VMs are heavy. Each one includes a full operating system, which can consume gigabytes of disk
space and significant amounts of RAM and CPU. They are slow to boot up, and because they are
so large, they are not easily portable.
Containers, on the other hand, offer a much more lightweight solution. Instead of virtualizing
the hardware, containers virtualize the operating system. This means that all containers
running on a single host machine share the same host OS kernel. The container only packages
the application code itself, along with its specific libraries and dependencies (the "userspace").
This fundamental difference makes containers incredibly efficient.
Figure 4.1: Comparing VMs and containers
79 Introduction to Containerization with Docker
The previous diagram compares the architectures of VMs and containers, highlighting how
containers achieve efficiency by sharing the host operating system instead of replicating it for
each instance. The VM side shows a host OS, a hypervisor, and multiple guest OSs, each with
its own bins/libs and app. The container side shows a host OS, a container engine (such as
Docker), and multiple containers that share the host OS kernel, each with just their own bins/
libs and app.
Think of it like this: a VM is like a single-family house. It's completely self-contained with its
own plumbing, electrical system, and foundation. It provides great isolation but is expensive
and slow idx_48d94e1f to build. A container is like an apartment in idx_e9122832 a high-rise building. Each apartment is
an isolated, private space for its residents, but they all share the building's core infrastructure
(foundation, plumbing, and electricity). This is far more efficient, allowing you to fit many
more residents (applications) on the same piece of land (host machine).
This idx_690c7424 lightweight architecture gives containers their key advantages:
Speed: Containers can be started and stopped in seconds, as there is no separate OS to
boot.
Efficiency: Because they share the host kernel and don't need a guest OS, you can run
many more containers on a given host than you could VMs.
Portability: A container packages everything an application needs to run into a single,

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 78
chunks.content:
portable unit that is guaranteed to run the same way on any machine that can run
Docker. This is the ultimate solution to the "it works on my machine" problem.
Now that you understand what containers are and why they're so powerful, let's put that
knowledge into practice by building your first Docker image using a Dockerfile.
Hands-on: Building your first Docker image with a
Dockerfile
The two core idx_9656b714 concepts you need to grasp are the Docker image and idx_318212f5 the Dockerfile. A Docker
image is a read-only template that idx_2c6352b3 contains the application code, libraries, dependencies, and
other files needed for an application to run. You can think of it as a blueprint or a recipe. A
container is a runnable instance of an image. You can create many containers from the same
image. The Dockerfile is a simple text file that contains the step-by-step instructions for
building a Docker image.

Chapter 4 80
Step 1: Create a simple web application
We need an application to containerize. Let's create a very simple web server using Python and
the Flask idx_ee72a58f framework. You don't need to be a Python expert to follow along; this example is
chosen for its simplicity:
Navigate to your devops-book-projects directory and create a new project folder:
cd ~/devops-book-projects
mkdir simple-flask-app && cd simple-flask-app
Open this folder in VS Code.
Create a file named app.py and add the following code:
app.py
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)
@app.route('/')
def hello_world():
return 'Hello from inside a Docker Container!\n'
if __name__ == '__main__':
app.run(debug=True, host='0.0.0.0', port=8080)
Create another file named requirements.txt. This file lists the Python dependencies
our application needs:
requirements.txt
Flask==2.2.2
gunicorn==20.1.0
We are including Flask for the web framework and Gunicorn as a production-grade web server
to run our application inside the container.
Step 2: Write the Dockerfile
Now, let's idx_f26bc1f2 write the instructions to build an image for this application:
Create a new file in the root of your project named Dockerfile (no extension):
Dockerfile

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: 4.1 81 Introduction to Containerization with Docker
chunks.content:
4.1 81 Introduction to Containerization with Docker
Start from an official Python runtime as a parent image:
FROM python:3.9-slim
Set the working directory in the container:
WORKDIR /app
Copy the requirements file and install the dependencies:
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
Copy idx_08158ea6 the rest of the application source code:
COPY . .
Make port 8080 available to the world outside this container:

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: EXPOSE 8080
chunks.content:
EXPOSE 8080
Define the command to run your app using gunicorn:
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "app:app"]
Let's now deconstruct the Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.9-slim: Every Dockerfile must start with a FROM instruction. It specifies
the base image to build upon. We are starting from an official image that already has
Python 3.9 installed. The -slim tag refers to a minimal version of the image, which is a
best practice for keeping images small.
WORKDIR /app: This sets the working directory for any subsequent instructions. If the
directory doesn't exist, it will be created.
COPY requirements.txt .: This copies our dependencies file from our local project
directory into the working directory inside the image.
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt: The RUN instruction
executes a command inside the image during the build process. Here, we are using pip
to install our application's dependencies. This is a key optimization: by copying
requirements.txt and installing dependencies before copying the rest of our code,

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 82
chunks.content:
Chapter 4 82
Docker can cache this layer. If we change our application code later but not our
dependencies, Docker can reuse the cached layer, and the build will be much faster.
COPY . .: This copies the rest of our application's source code (such as app.py) into the
idx_76cae522 working directory. However, without any filtering, this instruction copies everything in
your project folder, including .git folders, local venv directories, and other files you
never want inside your image. The solution is a .dockerignore file. See the following
note for details.
EXPOSE 8080: This instruction informs Docker that the container listens on the
specified idx_e5ceafa7 network port at runtime. It's primarily for documentation and doesn't
actually publish the port.
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "app:app"]: This specifies the
default command to run when a container is started from this image. We are using
gunicorn to serve our Flask application (app:app means run the app object from the
app.py file).
•
Always use a .dockerignore file
A .dockerignore file works idx_99ac7810 exactly like .gitignore: it tells Docker which files
and folders to exclude from the build context (the files sent to the Docker
daemon when you run docker build). Without it, COPY . . risks bloating
your image with unnecessary files. Create a .dockerignore file in your project
root alongside the Dockerfile, with contents such as the following:
.git
__pycache__
*.pyc
venv/
.env
This keeps your image lean, avoids leaking sensitive files (such as .env with
credentials), and speeds up every build by reducing the amount of data
transferred to the Docker daemon.
Note
•
•
83 Introduction to Containerization with Docker
Step 3: Build the image
With our idx_ae106b86 Dockerfile complete, we can now build our image. Open your terminal in the root of
the simple-flask-app project directory.
Use the docker build command. The -t flag allows us to tag the image with a human-
readable name. The period (.) at the end tells Docker to look for the Dockerfile in the current
directory:
docker build -t simple-flask-app .
Docker will now execute each instruction in your Dockerfile one by one, creating a new layer
for each step. You will see the output of each command in your terminal. Once it's finished, you
have successfully built your first Docker image!
Development versus production — and what CI does with this
Dockerfile
Right now, you idx_6e03ccb8 are running docker build manually from your terminal; this is your
development workflow. In a idx_c837ee2a professional production workflow, this idx_08b15b83 exact same Dockerfile
will idx_c9b8212b be built automatically by a continuous integration (CI) pipeline every time you push
code to your Git repository. The pipeline pulls your code, runs docker build, executes tests

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 82
chunks.content:
inside the resulting image, and if everything passes, pushes the image to a registry such as
Docker Hub. This is the build-test-push cycle that sits at the heart of every modern DevOps
pipeline, and you'll build exactly that in a later chapter. For now, the key takeaway is that the
Dockerfile you write locally is the same artifact that runs in CI; write it well once, and it works
everywhere.
You've built an image, which is the blueprint. Now, it's time to bring it to life by running it as a
container.
Managing containers and images
In this idx_e663b659 section, you'll learn the essential commands for running, inspecting, stopping, and
idx_8829605d cleaning up both containers and the images they are built from. These are the day-to-day
commands you'll use constantly when working with Docker.
Running your first container
To run a idx_d5300dca container from your newly created image, you use the docker run command:
docker run -p 4000:8080 -d --name my-web-server simple-flask-app

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 84
chunks.content:
Chapter 4 84
Let's understand the docker run command in detail:
-p 4000:8080: This is idx_b65936b5 the port mapping. The EXPOSE instruction in the Dockerfile
opened port 8080 inside the container, but it's not accessible from our host machine by
default. The -p flag maps a port on the host machine to a port in the container. Here, we
are mapping port 4000 on our local machine to port 8080 inside the container.
-d: This runs idx_72b66456 the container in detached mode. This means the container runs in the
background, and your terminal is free for other commands. Without this, the container
would run in the foreground, and its logs would take over your terminal.
--name my-web-server: This gives our container a custom, human-readable name. If
you don't provide a name, Docker will assign a random one.
simple-flask-app: This is the name of the image we want to run.
The command idx_196dd6fa will output a long string of characters, which is the unique idx_3f75cc57 ID of your new
container. Now, open a web browser and navigate to http://localhost:4000. You should see
the message, Hello from inside a Docker Container! You are now accessing a web server
running inside an isolated container on your machine.
Now that your container is running, let's see how to manage it.
Essential container management commands
Once your idx_1df9baa7 containers are up and running, you'll need to know how to monitor, manage, and
clean them up. Here are some essential Docker commands every DevOps engineer should
master:
docker ps: This command lists all currently running containers. You'll see your my-web-
server container, along with its ID, the image it's from, and the port mapping. To see
all containers, including stopped ones, use docker ps -a.
docker logs <container_name_or_id>: This command fetches the logs from a
container. This is incredibly useful for debugging. Let's see the logs from our server:
docker logs my-web-server
You should see the startup messages from Gunicorn.
docker stop <container_name_or_id>: This gracefully stops a running container:
docker stop my-web-server

If you run docker ps now, the container will be gone. If you run docker ps -a, you will
see that its status is Exited.
docker start <container_name_or_id>: This restarts a stopped container.
docker rm <container_name_or_id>: This removes a stopped container permanently.
You cannot remove a running container; you must stop it first:
docker rm my-web-server
Now that you know how to manage containers themselves, let's look at how to manage the
images they are built from, which form the foundation of every container.
Essential image management commands
Just as idx_0824f2fe you need to manage containers, you also need to manage the images they are created

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 84
chunks.content:
from:
docker images: This command lists all the Docker images you have on your local
machine. You should see your simple-flask-app image, as well as the python:3.9-
slim image that it was built from.
docker rmi <image_name_or_id>: This removes an image from your local machine.
You cannot remove an image if there is a container (even a stopped one) that is using it.
You must remove the container first.
Mastering these few commands (run, ps, logs, stop, rm, images, and rmi) will give you the
ability to handle most day-to-day Docker tasks.
So far, you've worked with single containers, but real-world applications often rely on multiple
services running together. In the next section, we'll explore Docker Compose, a tool that lets
you define and manage multi-container applications with ease.
Using Docker Compose for multi-container
applications
Our simple web server runs nicely in a single container. However, most real-world applications
idx_d4bfdfcd are not so simple. They are often composed of multiple, interconnected services. For example,
you might have a web frontend, a backend API, a database, and a caching service. Managing
the lifecycle of all these containers individually with docker run commands would be complex
and tedious. This is where Docker Compose comes in.
Docker Compose is idx_0a332e2e a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications. It
uses idx_cbf95c05 a simple configuration file, written in a format called YAML, to configure all of your
•
•
•
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 4 86
chunks.content:
Chapter 4 86
application's services, networks, and volumes. With a single command, you can then create
and start all the services from your configuration.
Creating a docker-compose.yml file
Let's idx_55bc263e use Docker idx_39ec21ac Compose to define our simple web application. In the root of your simple-
flask-app project, create a new file named docker-compose.yml:
docker-compose.yml
version: '3.8'
services:
web:
build: .
ports:
- "4000:8080"
volumes:
- .:/app
Let's deconstruct the Compose file:
version: '3.8': This specifies the version of the Compose file format we are using.
Note that as of Docker Compose v2, the version key is considered optional and may
generate a warning in newer installations; it is safe to omit it in modern projects.
services: This is the main key where we define all the different containers that make
up our application.
docker compose versus docker-compose
Which command should I use? Docker originally shipped Compose as a separate
Python tool invoked as docker-compose (with a hyphen). Since Docker Desktop 3.4
and Docker Engine 20.10, Compose is bundled directly into the Docker CLI as a
subcommand: docker compose (with a space). The new plugin form is the current
standard and is what Docker recommends for all new work. If you installed Docker
Desktop recently, use docker compose up and docker compose down. The
hyphenated docker-compose still works on systems where the standalone tool is
installed, but it is considered legacy.
Note
•
•
87 Introduction to Containerization with Docker
web: This is the name we are giving to our first service. You can name it anything you
like.
build: .: Instead of specifying an image name, this tells Docker Compose to build the
image from the Dockerfile located in the current directory (.).
ports: This is the same as the -p flag in docker run. It maps port 4000 on the host to
port 8080 in the container.
volumes: This is a new and very powerful feature. A volume mounts a directory from
your host machine into the container. This creates a live link between the two. .:/app
mounts the current project directory on our host machine (.) to the /app directory
inside the container. Now, if you change a file on your host machine, it will be instantly
reflected inside the running container! This is fantastic for development, as you no
longer need to rebuild your image for every single code change.
With idx_ab0ba3fa your docker-compose.yml file defined, you're now ready to put Docker Compose into
idx_f82bd4b2 action and see how it simplifies running multi-container applications.
Running the application with Compose
With the docker-compose.yml file in place, running our application becomes incredibly
simple. Make idx_975144c3 sure you have stopped and removed any containers you started earlier with
docker run:

chunks.content:
From the root of your project directory in the terminal, run the following command:
docker-compose up
Docker Compose will first build your image (if it's not already built) and then start the
web service container. Because we didn't use a -d flag, it will run in the foreground, and
you will see the logs directly in your terminal.
Go to http://localhost:4000 in your browser to see the application running.
Now, for the magic of volumes. Keep the server running. Open app.py in VS Code and
change the message from Hello from inside a Docker Container! to Hello from
Docker Compose! and save the file.

Refresh your browser. You will see the new message instantly, without having to
rebuild or restart anything!
To stop the application, go back to your terminal and press Ctrl + C. Then, to clean up
and remove the containers and networks created by Compose, run the following:
docker-compose down
Docker Compose simplifies the management of complex applications, making your
development workflow faster and more efficient. It is an indispensable tool for local
development with containers.
Now idx_26f03993 that you've learned how to build and run containers locally using Docker Compose, the
next step is to share your work with others. In the following section, we'll push your first image
to Docker Hub so it can be accessed and deployed anywhere.
Pushing your first image to Docker Hub
You have successfully built a Docker image and run it on your local machine. This is a huge
step, but the idx_5a24d433 true power of Docker is in its portability. To share your application with others or
to deploy it to a server, you need to put your image in a place idx_a734b090 where others can access it. This
place is called an image registry.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: 5.6 Troubleshooting common Compose issues
chunks.content:
5.6 Troubleshooting common Compose issues
Port already in use: If you see Bind for 0.0.0.0:4000 failed: port is already
allocated, another process (or a previous container) is using that port. Run docker ps
to find and stop any lingering containers, or change the host port in your docker-
compose.yml file (e.g., 5000:8080).
Changes not reflected after edit: If you change the Dockerfile or requirements.txt
file and the changes don't appear after restarting, force a rebuild: docker compose up
--build.
Container exits immediately: Run docker compose logs web to read the container's
output. The error message there will almost always tell you exactly what went wrong: a
missing module, a bad port binding, or an application crash.
Note
89 Introduction to Containerization with Docker
An image registry is a storage system for your Docker images. The most common and default
public registry is Docker Hub. It's like GitHub, but for Docker images. By pushing your image
to Docker Hub, you make it available for anyone in the world to pull and run.
Step 1: Tagging your image
Before you can push an image to Docker Hub, you need to tag it with a name that includes your
Docker idx_0e271c41 Hub username. This is how Docker Hub knows which account the image belongs to:
First, make sure you have a Docker Hub account. If not, sign up at https://
hub.docker.com/signup.
Use the docker tag command to create an alias for your existing image. The format is
docker tag <source_image> <your_dockerhub_username>/
<repository_name>:<tag>:
docker tag simple-flask-app yourusername/simple-flask-app:1.0.0
* Replace yourusername with your actual Docker Hub username. The :1.0.0 part is a
version tag, which is a crucial best practice for managing different versions of your
image.
Run docker images now. You will see your new, fully-qualified image name listed
alongside idx_aa7c0abe the original one. They are the exact same image, just with different tags.
Step 2: Logging in to Docker Hub
From your idx_2501422a terminal, you need to log in to your Docker Hub account:
docker login
It will prompt you for your username and password. Enter the credentials you used to sign up
for Docker Hub.
1.
2.
For CI/CD systems and automated scripts, you should not use your password directly.
Instead, you should idx_8fa0892e create and use a personal access token (PAT) from the Docker Hub
security settings.

Step 3: Pushing the image
With your idx_6621e1bd image tagged and your client logged in, you can now push the image to Docker Hub
with the docker push command:
docker push yourusername/simple-flask-app:1.0.0
Docker will upload the layers of your image to the registry. Once it's complete, you can go to
your Docker Hub account in your web browser, and you will see your new simple-flask-app
repository listed!
Now, anyone, on any machine with Docker installed, can run your exact application with a
single command:
docker run -p 4000:8080 yourusername/simple-flask-app:1.0.0
You have successfully containerized an application and shared it with the world. This
workflow (build, run, push) is a fundamental pattern in DevOps.
Summary
In this chapter, you have taken a massive leap into the world of modern software delivery by
mastering the fundamentals of containerization with Docker. You started by understanding
the "why", learning how containers solve the chronic "it works on my machine" problem by

Code with Terraform
In the previous chapter, you learned how to package your application and all its dependencies
into a portable, consistent Docker container. You now have a reliable artifact that is guaranteed
to run the same way everywhere. This solves a massive piece of the software delivery puzzle.
But it also raises the next logical question: where do we run this container? An application needs
infrastructure, servers, networks, databases, and load balancers to function. How do we create
and manage this infrastructure in a way that is as reliable, version-controlled, and automated
as our application code?
The idx_6a2aaa1b answer is Infrastructure as Code (IaC), a practice that is as fundamental to DevOps as
version control and containerization. This chapter will introduce you to idx_d9c65ac5 the world of IaC and to
its most popular tool: Terraform. You will learn how to move away from manual, error-prone
infrastructure management and instead define your cloud resources in simple, declarative
configuration files. We will cover the core concepts of Terraform, including providers,
resources, and the critical state file. You will then get hands-on, writing your first Terraform
code to provision, modify, and destroy real resources in the cloud. Finally, you'll learn how to
make your code reusable and dynamic using variables and outputs. By the end of this chapter,
you will be able to manage your infrastructure with the same rigor and confidence as you
manage your application code.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
What is IaC?
Terraform fundamentals: Providers, resources, and state
Hands-on: Writing Your first Terraform configuration file

Using terraform plan and terraform apply to provision cloud resources
Managing variables and outputs for reusable code
Technical requirements
For this chapter, you will need the cloud account you created in Chapter 2. We will use AWS for
our hands-on examples, so please ensure your AWS Free Tier account is active. You will also
need your code editor (VS Code) and terminal. The main new tool for this chapter is Terraform,
and we will walk through its installation together.
What is IaC?
Before we dive into Terraform, let's establish what IaC is and why it's so revolutionary. For
many years, managing IT infrastructure was a manual, artisanal process. If a developer needed
a new server, they would file a ticket. An operations engineer would then manually log in to a
idx_18ed29b1 server rack or a cloud provider's web console, click through a series of wizards, and configure
the server by hand. This manual approach, often called click-ops, was idx_958c0714 slow, inconsistent, and
fraught with human error.
IaC is the practice of managing and provisioning computer data centers through machine-

chunks.heading: Chapter 4 92
chunks.content:
readable definition files, rather than physical hardware configuration or interactive
configuration tools. It means writing code to define, deploy, and update your infrastructure.
Instead of clicking in a web console to create a virtual machine, you write a block of code that
defines idx_fe531cd4 the properties of that machine. This simple shift in approach has profound benefits:
Automation and speed: IaC allows you to automate the entire infrastructure
provisioning process. You can spin up a complete production environment—with
servers, databases, networks, and firewalls—in minutes, a task that would have taken
days or weeks of manual effort.
Consistency and reliability: Manual processes lead to inconsistencies. Two servers
configured by hand will never be exactly identical. This configuration drift is a major
source of bugs. With IaC, every environment is provisioned from the same source code,
guaranteeing that your development, testing, and production environments are
identical and eliminating a huge class of "it works on my machine" problems.
Version control and collaboration: Because your infrastructure is defined in code, you
can store it in a Git repository, just like your application code. This means you get a full
version history of your infrastructure. Who changed the firewall rules? When? Why?
With IaC and Git, you can answer these questions instantly. It also idx_04d7ca12 enables

collaboration through pull requests and code reviews, allowing the entire team to have
visibility and input into infrastructure changes.
Cost savings: By automating setup and teardown, you can easily create ephemeral
environments for testing or development and destroy them when you're done,
ensuring you only pay for the resources you are actively using.
With a clear understanding of what IaC is and why it matters, the next step is to examine the
two main ways it can be implemented: the declarative and imperative approaches.
Declarative versus imperative IaC
There idx_e2e1d951 are two main approaches to IaC:
An imperative approach is like idx_52bfb5a9 giving someone a recipe. You idx_4094a3a9 define the exact steps
required to get to the desired state—for example, "First, create a virtual machine.
Second, attach a 10GB disk to it. Third, install Apache on it." Tools such as Ansible and
Chef often use an imperative style.
A declarative approach is like idx_0b9025a4 showing someone a blueprint. You idx_b2636531 define the desired
end state, and the IaC tool is responsible for figuring out the steps to get there—for
example, "I want one virtual machine with these specifications and a 10 GB disk, and it
must have Apache installed." Terraform is a declarative tool.
You tell Terraform what you want your infrastructure to look like, and Terraform handles the
logic of creating, updating, or deleting resources to match your definition. This is an incredibly
powerful model because it allows you to focus on the what instead of the how, and it makes
managing the state of your infrastructure over time much simpler.
You have now understood the core approaches to IaC. Let's move on to how Terraform
implements these ideas in practice by exploring its key building blocks.
Terraform fundamentals: Providers, resources, and
state
Terraform, created by HashiCorp, is an open source IaC tool that has become the industry
standard for idx_9ba9ca1a provisioning and managing cloud infrastructure. It idx_cc047530 uses a simple, human-
readable configuration language called HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL). Before we
write our first line of HCL, we need to understand three core concepts that are fundamental to
how Terraform works: providers, resources, and state.
•
•
•
95 Introduction to Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
Providers: The plugins for APIs
Terraform is cloud-agnostic, meaning it can manage infrastructure across hundreds of
different idx_fb1b775f platforms and services. It achieves this through a plugin-based idx_64adb047 architecture called
providers. A provider is responsible for understanding the API of a specific service, such as
AWS, Azure, GCP, or even GitHub and Docker, and exposing its components as resources that
you can use in your code.

When you start a new Terraform project, you declare which providers you intend to use. When
you run terraform init, Terraform automatically downloads and installs the correct provider
plugins for you. For example, if you want to create an S3 bucket in AWS, you will declare that
you are using the aws provider. The aws provider knows how to make the necessary API calls to
AWS to create, read, update, and delete S3 buckets.
Resources: The building blocks of infrastructure
A resource is the idx_00695c84 most important element in the Terraform language. Each resource idx_a8d08321 block
describes one or more infrastructure objects, such as a virtual network, a compute instance, or
a DNS record. A resource block has two parts:
Resource type: The idx_94221090 resource type is defined by idx_31b7f5e2 the provider (e.g., aws_s3_bucket)
Local name: The idx_a3f689f2 local name is a name you choose idx_80426410 to refer to this resource within your
Terraform code (e.g., app_bucket)
Here is the basic syntax for a resource:
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app_bucket" {
bucket = "my-unique-devops-book-bucket-12345"
tags = {
Name = "My DevOps Bucket"
Environment = "Dev"
}
}
This code idx_17464f6e block tells Terraform that we want to ensure an S3 idx_33cc103f bucket exists with the name my-
unique-devops-book-bucket-12345. The block's body contains the configuration arguments
for the resource, such as its name and any tags.

State: The map to the real world
This is arguably idx_085f48ab the most critical concept in Terraform. After Terraform creates a resource in
the real idx_c734688c world, how does it keep track of it? The answer idx_a910a98b is the state file. Terraform creates and
maintains a file named terraform.tfstate that stores a mapping between the resources
defined in your code and the real-world objects that have been created.
This state file is crucial for several reasons:
Mapping: It's how idx_0158cd32 Terraform knows that the resource named app_bucket in your code
corresponds to the actual S3 bucket with the ID my-unique-devops-book-
bucket-12345 in your AWS account.
Performance: When idx_65ea6a5b you run Terraform again, it can check the state file to see what
already exists, preventing it from having to query the cloud provider for every single
resource, which can be slow.
Planning: Before idx_a05720e6 making any changes, Terraform reads the state file to understand the
current state of your infrastructure. It then compares this to the desired state defined in
your code and creates a plan to bridge the gap.
S3 remote backend
The state file is a sensitive file. It contains details about your infrastructure and can sometimes
idx_b7e04f65 include secrets. By default, it is stored as a local file named terraform.tfstate. For any real
project, you should never commit this file to Git. You should also exclude the .terraform
directory, which contains downloaded provider binaries and is regenerated by terraform
init. Add a .gitignore file to your project root containing, at minimum, the following:
.terraform/
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.backup
Instead, you should idx_6f9747bb configure a remote backend to store the state file securely and provide
locking to prevent multiple team members from running Terraform simultaneously and
corrupting the state. A minimal S3 backend configuration looks like this:
terraform {
backend "s3" {
bucket = "my-terraform-state-bucket"
key = "global/s3/terraform.tfstate"
region = "us-east-1"

Using terraform plan and terraform apply to
provision cloud resources
You've idx_a98693a8 written the code that idx_b9f1ae4c describes your desired idx_64e3c688 infrastructure. Now, let's idx_f106852c use the core
Terraform workflow to make it a reality. This workflow consists of three main commands:
init, plan, and apply.
Step 1: Initialize the project with terraform init
The first idx_5d001729 command you must run in any new Terraform project is terraform init. This
command looks at your configuration files, determines which providers you need, and
downloads them into a hidden .terraform directory.
In your terminal, at the root of your project, run the following:
terraform init
Terraform will find the aws provider declaration and download it for you. You only need to run
this command once per project, or whenever you add a new provider.
Step 2: Preview changes with terraform plan
This is idx_beeed5fa the most important safety feature in Terraform. The terraform plan command creates
an execution plan. It reads your code, compares it to the current state (which is empty right
now), and shows you exactly what actions it would take to achieve the desired state, without
actually doing anything.
S3 bucket names must be globally unique across all of AWS. You will need to change the
bucket name in the preceding code to something unique to you, or Terraform will fail.
Note
101 Introduction to Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
Run the plan command:
terraform plan
You will see a color-coded output:
A + symbol in green means a resource will be created.
A – symbol in red means a resource will be destroyed.
A ~ symbol in yellow means a resource will be modified in-place.
The plan will show that it intends to create one new resource: your aws_s3_bucket. Always
review the plan carefully before proceeding.
Drift detection
One of Terraform's most powerful capabilities is detecting configuration drift, when the real
state of idx_13257c9e your infrastructure no longer matches what your code describes. This can happen if
someone makes a manual change in the AWS console. If you run terraform plan after such a
manual change, Terraform will compare the live state of your AWS account against your code
and flag the discrepancy with a ~ (modify) or -/ + (replace) symbol. Running terraform apply
would then reconcile the infrastructure back to the state described in your code. This
declarative correction is what gives IaC its power: your code is always the single source of
truth.

In professional teams, terraform plan is not just a local safety check. It is typically run
automatically idx_eb8eeec6 by a CI pipeline when a pull request is opened against your infrastructure
repository. The plan output is posted as a comment on the pull request, giving reviewers a
clear, human-readable preview of every resource that would be created, modified, or destroyed
if the pull request were merged. This turns infrastructure changes into a reviewable artifact,
applying the same pull request discipline to your cloud resources that you already use for
application code. Tools such as Atlantis and Terraform Cloud provide native support for this
workflow.
Step 3: Apply the changes with terraform apply
Once idx_6c91fbba you are satisfied with the plan, you can tell Terraform to execute it using the terraform
apply command. This is the command that makes real changes to your infrastructure.
Run the apply command:
terraform apply

Managing variables and outputs for reusable code
In our idx_3ddd6235 first example, we hardcoded values such idx_87f651ed as the region and the idx_fc61729a bucket name directly into
our main.tf file. This is fine for a simple test, but for real projects, it's a bad practice. It makes
the code inflexible and difficult to reuse. Terraform provides two powerful constructs to solve
this: input variables and output values.
Parameterizing your code with input variables
An input variable allows you idx_d0276e6f to pass values into your Terraform configuration idx_a38095b6 from the
outside, making your code reusable and dynamic. Let's refactor our S3 bucket code to use
variables:
Create a new file named variables.tf. It's a best practice to define all your variables in
a separate file:
variables.tf
variable "aws_region" {
description = "The AWS region to create resources in."
type = string
default = "us-east-1"
}
variable "bucket_name" {
description = "The name of the S3 bucket."
type = string
}
Here we've defined two variables. aws_region has a default value, so it's optional to
provide. bucket_name does not, so Terraform will require you to provide a value for it.

Displaying information with output values
After idx_541e838a Terraform creates a resource, you often want to idx_ac3b5441 see some of its attributes, such as a

Understanding CI and CD
We briefly introduced CI and CD as phases in the DevOps lifecycle in Chapter 1. Now, we must
understand them in greater detail, not just as phases, but as disciplines that are central to the
DevOps philosophy. They are the practical implementation of the core principles of
automation, fast feedback, and continuous improvement. Let's start with Continuous
Integration.
Continuous Integration: The discipline of frequent merging
CI is a development practice where developers frequently, often multiple times a day, merge
their code idx_3d541d6d changes into a central repository. After each merge, an automated build and test
sequence is triggered. The primary goal of CI is to detect integration issues as early as possible.
Think back to the pre-CI era, where developers would work in isolation on long-lived feature
branches for weeks. When it was finally time to merge everything together, the result was
often "merge hell," a painful, time-consuming process of resolving countless conflicts and
subtle bugs that only appeared when different pieces of code interacted. CI was created to
solve this problem. By integrating in small, frequent batches, the process becomes simple and
low-risk.

Chapter 6 112
A successful CI practice is built on a simple, powerful feedback loop:
A developer commits a change to a branch.
They open a pull request or push the commit to the central repository.
This automatically triggers a CI server.
The CI server runs a predefined process: it builds the application (compiling code,
packaging artifacts) and runs a suite of automated tests (unit tests, integration tests,
etc.).
The server provides immediate feedback. If the build or any test fails, the team is notified
instantly. The highest priority then becomes fixing the build.
The benefits idx_880067ab of this discipline are immense. It prevents integration problems from spiraling out
of control, improves code quality by ensuring a baseline of tests always pass, and allows teams
to develop faster and with greater confidence. CI is the foundation upon which all other
delivery automation is built.
While CI focuses on merging and testing code frequently, the next step in the delivery pipeline
is getting that tested code into production. This is where Continuous Delivery and Continuous
Deployment come into play.
Continuous Delivery versus Continuous Deployment
CD is the logical extension of CI. It's a practice where you automate the entire software release
idx_81ec8ecb process. With CD, every change that passes the automated tests is automatically deployed to a
testing or staging idx_73f00a7e environment. The result is that, at any given moment, you have a version of
your application that has been fully tested and is ready to be deployed to production.
The key aspect of CD is that the final step, deploying to the actual production environment, is
still a manual, push-button decision. A product manager or team lead can decide when to
release to customers. This separates the technical release from the business release, providing
control and flexibility.
Continuous Deployment, on the idx_cd865d5d other hand, takes this one step further. With Continuous
Deployment, every change that passes all stages of your production pipeline is automatically
released to your customers. There is no human intervention. This is a more advanced practice
that requires a very high degree of confidence in your automated testing and monitoring.
The following diagram illustrates the CI/CD pipeline, showing how CI flows seamlessly into
CD and Continuous Deployment, from code and testing to release and operation:

4.5 113 Constructing Your First CI/CD Pipeline

For the rest idx_df031b23 of this book, we idx_8efc4018 will focus on achieving CD. It provides the perfect balance of
automation and control for most teams. Together, CI and CD create the pipeline, an automated
assembly line that moves your code from idea to a deployable artifact safely and efficiently.
Now that you understand the principles behind CI and CD, it's time to see how they're
implemented in practice. In the next section, we'll explore GitHub Actions, a powerful
automation tool that brings CI/CD workflows directly into your code repository.
Introduction to GitHub Actions for automation
To implement a CI/CD pipeline, you idx_5f699021 need an automation server. There are idx_c359281b many great tools
available, such as Jenkins, CircleCI, and GitLab CI. For this book, we will use GitHub Actions, a
powerful and flexible CI/CD platform built directly into GitHub. Its tight integration with your
source code makes it incredibly easy to get started with automation.
Core concepts of GitHub Actions
GitHub Actions is built around a few core concepts that you define in a special type of file.
Before we idx_e90a68c9 create our first workflow, let's review the key components that make up GitHub
Actions and understand how they work together to automate your development process:
Workflow: A workflow is an automated process that you define. It is composed of one
or more jobs and is triggered by an event. Workflows are defined using YAML files and
must be stored in a specific directory in your repository: .github/workflows/.
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 6 114
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 114
Event: An event is a specific activity that triggers a workflow run. The most common
events are push (when someone pushes commits to a branch) and pull_request (when
a pull request is opened or updated). But there are many others, including manual
triggers and scheduled timers.
Job: A job is a set of steps that execute on the same runner. By default, jobs in a
workflow run in parallel. You can also configure jobs to be dependent on each other and
run sequentially.
Step: A step is an individual task that can run commands or an action. Steps within a
job are executed in order and are dependent on each other.
Action: An action is a reusable, standalone command that you can use as a step in your
job. Many common tasks, such as checking out your code (actions/checkout) or
setting up a specific version of a programming language (actions/setup-python), are
available as pre-built actions from the GitHub Marketplace. This saves you from having
to write complex scripts for common tasks.
Runner: A runner is a server that has the GitHub Actions runner application installed.
This is the machine that will execute your jobs. GitHub provides and maintains idx_1096e696 runners
for you (GitHub-hosted runners) with various operating systems (Ubuntu, Windows,
macOS). You can also host your own runners if you need a custom environment.
By combining these simple building blocks, you can create sophisticated workflows to
automate almost any aspect of your software development lifecycle.
Now that you understand the core components of GitHub Actions, let's put them into practice
by building a simple CI pipeline that automatically tests your code whenever changes are
pushed to the repository.
Hands-on: Building a simple CI pipeline to test code
automatically
Let's build idx_9e0299e2 our first pipeline. Our goal is to create a CI workflow that automatically runs tests
on our Flask application from Chapter 4 every time we push a change to our repository. This
will provide immediate feedback on whether our changes have broken anything.

pytest framework:

branches: [ "main" ]

branches: [ "main" ]

- name: Set up Python 3.9

python-version: '3.9'
- name: Install dependencies

python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt
- name: Run tests with pytest

Push your changes to your main branch on GitHub.
git push origin main
Now, go to your repository on GitHub and click on the Actions tab. You will see your
"Continuous Integration" workflow running! You can click on it to see the live output of
each step. After a minute or two, you should see a green checkmark, indicating that
your tests passed and the workflow was successful.
You have just created a safety net for your project. From now on, every time you or a teammate
pushes code, you will get immediate, automated feedback on its quality. If a workflow idx_b21c1b18 run fails,
GitHub Actions gives you several tools to diagnose the problem: click on the failed run in the
Actions tab to expand each step and read its full log output, which typically shows the exact
error message and the line that caused it. Once you have identified and fixed the issue, you can
push a new commit to trigger the workflow again, or, for transient failures such as a flaky
network dependency, use the Re-run jobs button on the Run page to retry without any code
change.
Now that you have a working CI pipeline to automatically test your code, the next step is to
extend this automation to deployment. In the following section, we'll configure a CD pipeline
to automatically deploy your application to a staging environment.
Configuring a CD pipeline to deploy to a staging
environment
We will idx_c00db386 now build a CD pipeline. This pipeline will trigger after a change is merged into the
main branch. It will build our Flask application into a Docker image, push that image to a
container registry, and then deploy that image to a staging environment running on AWS App
Runner. Let's get started.
Step 1: Set up AWS ECR and GitHub secrets
First, we idx_d7dab2a9 need a place to store our Docker images. We will idx_75d651cb use Amazon Elastic Container
Registry (ECR), which is a fully managed Docker container registry provided by AWS. We will
also need a secure way to give our GitHub Actions workflow permission to access our AWS
account.
Create an ECR repository: In the AWS Management Console, navigate to the ECR
service. Click Create repository. Keep it Private and give it a name – for example,
simple-flask-app.

Create an IAM user for GitHub Actions: In the IAM service, create a new user. Give it
programmatic access. Attach the AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPowerUser and
AWSAppRunnerFullAccess permissions. Save the access key ID and secret access key.
As a security best practice, follow the principle of least privilege: rather than attaching
broad managed policies, consider creating a custom IAM policy that grants only the
specific actions your pipeline actually needs, such as ecr:GetAuthorizationToken,
ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability, ecr:PutImage, and the minimum App Runner
actions required. This limits the blast radius if credentials are ever accidentally
exposed.
Configure GitHub secrets: In your GitHub repository, go to Settings > Secrets and
variables > Actions. Click New repository secret. Create two secrets:
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: Paste the access key ID you just created.
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: Paste the secret access key.
GitHub idx_0f633d49 secrets are encrypted and provide a secure way to store sensitive information such as
passwords and API keys for use in your workflows.
Step 2: Create the Terraform code for AWS App Runner
We will idx_17de105d use Terraform to manage our staging environment. AWS App Runner is a service that
makes it incredibly easy to deploy containerized applications.
Create a new directory in your project called terraform.
Inside terraform, create a main.tf file with the following code. This defines an App
Runner service that will pull its image from our ECR repository.
terraform/main.tf
terraform {
required_providers {
aws = {
source = "hashicorp/aws"
version = "~> 4.0"
}
}
}
provider "aws" {
region = "us-east-1"
}

Enhancing pipelines with generative AI for workflow
automation
As we've idx_f3eecb95 just seen, writing idx_692bc43a CI/CD pipelines involves scripting, configuration, and a deep
understanding of the tools involved. This is an area where generative AI is emerging as a
powerful assistant for the DevOps engineer. While AI won't replace the need for you to
understand the fundamentals, it can significantly accelerate your workflow, improve quality,
and help you manage complexity.

AI as a development and automation accelerator
One idx_461845b7 of the most direct applications of AI is in writing the code and configuration for the
pipeline itself. Tools idx_cf7a1bfb such as GitHub Copilot, which are integrated directly into editors such as
VS Code, act as an expert pair programmer. As you start typing your ci.yml file, Copilot can
provide intelligent, context-aware suggestions for entire steps or even complete jobs. You
might type a comment such as # Step to build and push to ECR, and Copilot can generate
the corresponding YAML, complete with the correct action names, environment variables, and
login commands, saving you from having to look up documentation and reducing syntax
errors.
This idx_84bb1934 assistance extends beyond the pipeline configuration. AI can help generate unit tests for
your application code, increasing your test coverage and the effectiveness of your CI quality
gate. It can also help write your Dockerfile or Terraform configurations, suggesting best
practices for security and efficiency.
Automated quality and security gates
Perhaps the most exciting frontier is AI-powered code review. New tools are emerging that can
idx_1dbb6fde be integrated directly into your pull request process. These AI reviewers can automatically scan
your code for common bugs, security idx_fadae552 vulnerabilities (DevSecOps), and style inconsistencies,
providing instant feedback before a human even needs to look at it. This acts as an initial,
automated quality gate, catching simple mistakes and allowing human reviewers to focus on
more complex architectural and logical aspects of a change.
Furthermore, AI can analyze the results of a test suite run. If a test fails, instead of just showing
a red X, an AI tool can analyze the logs and the code changes to suggest a probable root cause,
dramatically reducing the time it takes for a developer to debug and fix the issue.
Intelligent pipeline orchestration and communication
Generative idx_91e33a69 AI is also being used to automate the communication and documentation
surrounding the CI/CD process. For example, AI tools can be configured to do the following:
Generate clear commit messages: By analyzing the content of a code change, AI can
suggest a concise and well-formatted commit message that follows team conventions
Draft pull request descriptions: AI can summarize the changes in a pull request, list
the key files affected, and provide a starting point for the developer's explanation
Create automated release notes: For each new release, AI can parse the list of merged
pull requests and generate a human-readable summary of the new features, bug fixes,
and improvements, ready to be shared with stakeholders

Summary
In this chapter, you bridged the gap between code on your laptop and a running application in
the cloud by building your first fully automated CI/CD pipeline. You solidified your
understanding of Continuous Integration as a practice for ensuring quality and Continuous
Delivery as a practice for enabling reliable releases. You were introduced to the core concepts of
GitHub Actions, workflows, events, jobs, steps, and runners, as the building blocks of
automation.
You then put this knowledge into action. First, you built a practical CI pipeline that
automatically runs tests on every code change, creating a crucial safety net. Then, you
constructed a complete CD pipeline that took your containerized application, built and pushed
it to a container registry, and then used Terraform to automatically deploy it to a staging
environment on AWS App Runner. Finally, you looked ahead at how generative AI is set to
make these processes even faster and smarter. You have now built the automated assembly

Now that you have an automated pipeline, how do you manage the infrastructure part of that

In the last chapter, you constructed a complete CI/CD pipeline that automatically builds, tests,
and deploys your containerized application. You witnessed the power of automating the
application delivery process. However, you may have noticed a manual step remained: the
infrastructure that the application was deployed to had to exist beforehand. In a truly
automated DevOps environment, the creation and management of the infrastructure itself
should be part of the pipeline.
This chapter connects the two powerful pillars of automation you have learned about: CI/CD
and Infrastructure as Code (IaC). You idx_cc8a6722 will idx_f71eafc7 learn how to integrate Terraform directly into your
GitHub Actions workflows, creating a single, unified pipeline that manages both your
application and the infrastructure it runs on. We will build a workflow that automatically
provisions your staging environment whenever you make a change to your infrastructure code.
We will tackle the critical challenge of managing Terraform's state file in a collaborative
environment by configuring a secure, remote backend. You'll also learn how to implement
crucial safety features, such as manual approval gates, to control deployments to sensitive
environments. Finally, we'll explore how AI is making IaC even smarter by helping to detect
configuration drift and suggest optimizations.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
Integrating Terraform with GitHub Actions
Hands-on: Creating a workflow to automatically provision staging infrastructure
Managing Terraform state in a collaborative environment
Implementing a manual approval step for production deployments
Optimizing IaC with AI-driven suggestions and drift detection

Technical requirements
For this chapter, you will need everything from our previous hands-on sections, including your
GitHub repository, VS Code, and an active AWS Free Tier account. You should have Terraform
installed locally and your AWS credentials configured as secrets in your GitHub repository
(AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY). You can download the example project
and code for this book by following the instructions in the Download the example code files
section in the Preface of this book.
This chapter's code files are included in the downloadable code bundle.
Integrating Terraform with GitHub Actions
In Chapter 5, you idx_0246030d learned about the core Terraform idx_c724a577 workflow: init, plan, and apply. You ran

these commands from your local machine, which is perfect for learning and individual
development. However, in a team environment, running Terraform locally presents several
problems. What if a team member forgets to pull the latest code before applying a change?
What if two people try to apply conflicting changes at the same time? How do you review and
approve infrastructure changes before they happen?
The solution is to run Terraform from within your CI/CD pipeline. By integrating Terraform
with a tool such as GitHub Actions, you create a centralized, consistent, and auditable process
for managing your infrastructure.
Benefits of a GitOps approach to infrastructure
This practice of using a idx_c258d8c4 Git repository as the single source of truth for your infrastructure and
using a CI/CD pipeline to automatically apply changes is a core tenet of a workflow known as
GitOps. The benefits are transformative:
Single source of truth: Your Git repository contains the complete, desired state of your
infrastructure. There is no ambiguity about what should be running in production.
Auditability: Every change to your infrastructure is a commit in Git. You have a full,
immutable log of who changed what, when, and why.
Automated and consistent execution: The pipeline ensures that Terraform is always
run in the same clean, consistent environment, eliminating the "it works on my
machine" problem for infrastructure.
Collaboration and review: Infrastructure changes are proposed via pull requests.
This allows the entire team to review and discuss the proposed changes (terraform
plan output) before they are applied, dramatically reducing the risk of costly mistakes.
